beats.text: Why do flamingos rest on one leg?
beats.visual_intent: frame 0: flamingo on one leg in water, question mark

beats.text: In 2017, researchers propped up a dead flamingo.
beats.visual_intent: lab bench, X-eyed flamingo held upright by a clamp

beats.text: On one leg, it settled into a steady pose, with no muscle working.
beats.visual_intent: the X-eyed flamingo steady on one leg, check mark

beats.text: On two legs, it wouldn't stay steady.
beats.visual_intent: same flamingo on two legs, tipping, motion lines, a cross

beats.text: So one leg takes very little muscle effort.
beats.visual_intent: muscle meter near empty beside the one-legged flamingo

beats.text: Live birds at Zoo Atlanta swayed less when they dozed off.
beats.visual_intent: sleeping flamingo on a force plate, sway arcs shrink

beats.text: A 2010 zoo study adds a clue: more birds did it in water, and more as it got colder. That may save heat.
beats.visual_intent: flamingo in cold water, thermometer low, tucked leg under the feathers

beats.text: One leg isn't a balancing act. It's a flamingo's armchair.
beats.visual_intent: flamingo relaxing on one leg beside an armchair

beats.text: So next time you see one on one leg, it's probably resting.
beats.visual_intent: back to the one-legged flamingo, eyes closed, calm
